# Pool-member config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/members/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.MemberBlock` (ADR-092 D1/D2) declaring one **member** — one interchangeable thing a `pool` draws on. The block label is the member name.

**A member declaring only a `provides` map is a complete, useful declaration.** It is one of N interchangeable things, and it is the floor of the design rather than a degenerate case; `seats`, the expiry pair, and the capacity attributes later waves add, are optional refinements of it.

`provides` is what the member supplies to a dispatch that acquires it: freeform `NAME = "value"` attributes, where each `NAME` is a `credential_spec` field of the capability the dispatch invokes. That is the generalization of the retired `llm_account.type`, which named a *shape* and selected one hard-coded field from it; naming fields directly is what lets an egress-identity member supply `https_proxy`, a device member supply an endpoint, and a subscription member supply a token through one mechanism. A value may be a credential reference (`env://`, `keychain://`, `vault://`) **or a bare literal** — the literal is admitted for a non-secret (a proxy URL, a device name), and the consequence to author around is that `tera config pull` exports a literal verbatim into a vault-tracked file, so anything secret should be a reference.

**`provides` is optional, and an empty one means the member supplies *admission* rather than a value** (ADR-106 D5, amending ADR-092 D1): permission to run on this machine, with the seat itself the whole of what is handed out. That is what a fleet-host member declares — a dispatch draws one seat from **each** of the pools it needs, and a host pool's seat is consumed as a ceiling on the machine while the token pool beside it supplies the credential. D1 originally required at least one entry, on the ground that a member supplying nothing is not a member of anything a dispatch could use; what that rule was really protecting is the ledger charging a member for sessions that ran on the deployment's static fallback credential, and a host seat is charged for exactly what it bought.

**A member declaring `grant {}` is the one exception, and it is refused by name.** A grant means "adopt this token set once, then own and refresh it", so it needs exactly one `provides` entry — never zero — and that entry must be a credential reference naming the token *set* rather than a leaf field of it. A grant with nothing named has nothing to adopt, and it is rejected at `tera config apply` and `tera validate` rather than accepted and failed at the first refresh.

A name that matches no `credential_spec` field is rejected at `tera config apply` and `tera validate`, not at dispatch: at dispatch a wrong name and a legitimately-inapplicable one are indistinguishable, because a pooled Work Order's session invokes plenty of tools the member cannot fill and the overlay is right to drop those silently. A member in a pool nothing references yet has nothing to resolve against, and warns instead.

`seats` bounds concurrent leases and is **three-valued** (ADR-092 D3): `seats = 0` is a ceiling of zero — live, still in its pool, admitting nothing because it can hold nothing, which is a statement about capacity and not a drain (ADR-178 D7); `seats = n` bounds it at n; and an **unset** `seats` is *unbounded concurrency*, for a member with nothing to bound. Unset is not a synonym for either of the others, and all three reach the gate as themselves: a member with a ceiling of zero is never selected, a bounded one is selected up to `seats − reserved_seats` live leases, and an unbounded one is selected without a ceiling — so a pool of members declaring nothing but `provides` admits dispatches and rotates between them. `reserved_seats` is withheld from dispatch, implementing the enforcement-boundary decision of PRD-016 §9: a configured reservation is chosen over voluntary registration by an external supervisor, because tera cannot verify an external session's self-report anyway. It requires a **ceiling** to withhold from (a reservation against an unbounded member withholds nothing) and must not exceed it; equal to the ceiling reserves the whole member. **The ceiling is resolved rather than read off this block**: it is this member's own `seats`, or — for a member whose name joins to a declared `runner` — that machine's `seats`, which is where ADR-133 D4 put it. So a fleet host declares `reserved_seats` here beside `runner "m4" { seats = 8 }` and never restates the ceiling itself. The attribute stayed on the member rather than moving with the ceiling because a reservation is a *subtraction from* a ceiling rather than a ceiling — the same reason `weight` stayed — and because ADR-133 D5's per-class reservation must grow additively from where this attribute already is.

`weight` is this member's share of the pool's steady traffic under `selection = "least-loaded"`, which ranks members on live leases divided by weight. It is **optional and rarely authored**: unset defaults to the member's *dispatchable* seats (`seats − reserved_seats`), because a seat ceiling is already a statement of how much a member can absorb and ranking on the fraction reads it as a share — so two hosts declaring 6 and 4 seats converge on 6:4 with nothing written here. An **unbounded** member (no `seats`) defaults to weight 1: it declares no ceiling to read a share off, and taking the declaration literally would make its fraction zero at every occupancy and hand it the entire pool. Write an explicit weight only where "how many at once" and "what share of steady traffic" genuinely differ — a machine that can hold four concurrent runs but should receive a third of the queue. It must be between 1 and 1000000 — the floor because a member that can take no traffic has a ceiling of zero, `seats = 0`, and the ceiling because a weight is meaningful only against its siblings and an unbounded one would let the selection arithmetic overflow and silently invert the ordering. Unlike `reserved_seats` it does **not** require a ceiling, because a weight is the only way to state an unbounded member's share. It is ignored under `selection = "round-robin"`, which rotates and reads no load at all.

`expires_at` is the instant this member stops being usable at all (ADR-092 D8), and `warn_before` is how long before it the member starts reporting `expiring` (default `30d`). Both are optional; together they give the member a computed **state** — `valid` / `expiring` / `expired` — which is one thing with three views: the startup warning, the `expiry` object on every `tera seats list` row, and a `_sys` event a later wave publishes. `expires_at` is an RFC3339 **instant** and only that, because a *discovered* expiry is an instant and "discovered wins over declared" is only a comparison if the two are the same type; a bare date is rejected with an error naming the repair. **An expired member sorts LAST in selection and remains selectable** — a declared expiry is an operator assertion rather than a verified fact, so a fat-fingered date costs selection preference and never capacity, and the runtime's own refusal stays authoritative. It is not a capacity signal: an expiry is when the member *dies*, one-way and terminal, and never when its capacity *returns*. Note what it does not track — a credential reference resolves per dispatch and uncached, so rotating a token takes effect immediately while `expires_at` does not, which makes rotation a three-step ritual: mint, store, then update `expires_at`.

**A member may be owned by a person** (ADR-148 D7): `owner = "alice@example.com"` beside `connection = "<name>"`. The owner supplies the credential with `tera connections set <connection>`, so the operator declares the member and never handles the secret. The member holds no copy of it: `grant {}`, `credential_provider {}` and a `provides` credential reference are refused beside an owner, and no `provides` field maps to the connection. The owner is resolved through the user directory by the resolver a role binding's email uses. An owner that is a worker, not an email, unknown, claimed by more than one record, or not a person is refused at load and at `tera config plan`, and `tera validate`, which has no directory, reports it unresolvable. A live daemon resolves it for every draw, so an owner who stops resolving makes the member unavailable on `tera seats list`, never re-homed. A team member may name a `connection` too; one that names none keeps its derived connection.

A member is never named by a consumer. Workers and tool bindings reference a pool through the `seat_pool` attribute, which is what lets an operator drain, add, or rotate a member without editing a single worker recipe.

## Example

A minimal `members`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/members/example-member.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

member "example-member" {
  connection = "example-connection"

  provides {
    example-connection = "env://EXAMPLE_CREDENTIAL"
  }
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | Member name. The label a pool's member "<label>" {} block names; never referenced directly by a worker or a tool binding. For a FLEET-HOST member (one whose seat is permission to run on a machine) this must equal the label of the runner block declaring that host: the daemon writes the host's link state onto this member's meters under the runner's own advertised name, and there is deliberately no second attribute mapping the two (ADR-106 D13). An ADMISSION-ONLY member (one with no provides) whose name matches no declared runner is REFUSED at tera config apply, at boot and in tera validate (ADR-133 D2): its seat would admit work onto nothing, and before that refusal existed it did not fail loudly — the member simply never received a link report, read as unknown, and stayed selectable, leaving an unreachable machine eligible for dispatch. A member that DOES name a declared runner may not also state seats: a machine's ceiling is declared once, on the runner block (ADR-133 D4). |
| `provides` | block | no | — | — | — | What this member supplies to a dispatch that acquires it: freeform NAME = "value" attributes, where each NAME is a credential_spec field of the capability the dispatch invokes — or, on a team member that names a connection, that connection's own name, whose entry is the member's credential for it (ADR-152 D4): it fills no capability field, the dispatch's proxy presents it as the connection's holder, and it is judged against the connection rather than against any credential_spec. OPTIONAL, and legitimately empty (ADR-106 D5): an empty or absent provides means the member supplies ADMISSION rather than a value — permission to run on this machine, with the seat itself the whole of what is handed out — which is what a fleet-host member declares. Values may be credential references (env://, keychain://, vault://) or bare literals; prefer a reference for anything secret, because tera config pull exports a literal verbatim into a vault-tracked file. A member declaring grant {} must supply exactly ONE entry, never zero, and that entry must be a reference naming a token set: with nothing named there is nothing for the grant to adopt. A member naming a connection keys that one entry by the connection's name — a plugin connection's stem, not its key — as it does the entry a credential_provider {} establishes into. |
| `seats` | integer | no | — | — | — | Concurrent-lease ceiling. Three distinct states: seats = 0 is a ceiling of ZERO (live, still in its pool, admitting nothing because it can hold nothing — a statement about capacity, not a drain, ADR-178 D7); seats = n bounds it at n; unset is UNBOUNDED concurrency, for a member with nothing to bound. Unset is not a synonym for 0 and not a synonym for any n. This is a MEMBER's ceiling: a machine's is declared on its own runner block, and a member whose name matches a declared runner may not state this attribute as well (ADR-133 D4) — that pair is refused, naming both homes. |
| `reserved_seats` | integer | no | — | — | — | Seats withheld from dispatch for an external supervisor to draw on. Unset means zero. Requires a ceiling to withhold from — a reservation against an unbounded member withholds nothing — and must not exceed it; equal to the ceiling reserves the whole member. The ceiling is this member's own seats, or, for a member whose name joins to a declared runner, that machine's seats (ADR-133 D4): a fleet host declares reserved_seats here and its ceiling on the runner block. |
| `weight` | integer | no | — | — | — | This member's share of the pool's steady traffic under selection = "least-loaded", which ranks members on live leases divided by weight. Unset defaults to the member's DISPATCHABLE seats (seats minus reserved_seats), so two hosts declaring 6 and 4 seats converge on 6:4 with nothing authored here — write it only when "how many at once" and "what share of steady traffic" genuinely differ. An UNBOUNDED member (no seats) defaults to 1: it has no ceiling to read a share off, and inferring one would hand it the whole pool. Must be between 1 and 1000000 — a member that can take no traffic has a ceiling of zero, spelled seats = 0, and the upper bound is what keeps the selection arithmetic exact rather than a limit any fleet meets. Ignored under selection = "round-robin", which rotates and reads no load at all. |
| `expires_at` | string | no | — | — | — | The instant this member stops being usable at all (ADR-092 D8), as an RFC3339 instant with an offset — "2027-08-12T00:00:00Z". A bare date is rejected rather than accepted as midnight: a DISCOVERED expiry is an instant, and "discovered wins over declared" is only a comparison if the two are the same type. An expired member sorts LAST in selection and stays selectable — a declared expiry is an operator assertion, not a verified fact, so a wrong date costs selection preference and never capacity. It is not a meter: this is when the member dies, not when its capacity returns. Rotating a credential does not update this field; the reference resolves per dispatch and uncached, so rotation is mint, store, THEN update expires_at. |
| `warn_before` | string | no | `30d` | — | — | How long before expires_at this member reports EXPIRING (duration; Nd for whole days, e.g. 30d, plus the usual h/m/s). Unset selects 30d — sized to catch a human's attention cycle, because renewing a subscription bearer is a five-minute operator act rather than a procurement one. Legal without expires_at: D8's instant may be DISCOVERED rather than declared. It changes what is reported and warned about; it never changes what is selectable. |
| `grant` | block | no | — | — | — | Present: the daemon owns and refreshes this member's OAuth grant, and the member's single provides entry names the token SET it is adopted from (not a single field of it). Absent: the member supplies its provides values as they resolve, which for a bare access-token reference means nothing renews it. |
| `credential_provider` | block | no | — | — | — | How an operator establishes or re-establishes this member's credential with tera seats credential <member>. Absent: the member has no operator door — a dead credential is repaired at its source and, if the member is held, the hold must be lifted with tera seats credential --force. Declarable only by the system vault or by kernel bootstrap HCL: a provider runs a program on the daemon host, unsandboxed, and is handed a secret. |
| `owner` | string | no | — | — | — | The person whose credential this member is (ADR-148 D7), written as their email and resolved through the user directory by the same resolver a role binding's email uses. Set: an OWNED member. Its credential is the owner's own row for connection, which the owner supplies with tera connections set <connection>; the operator declares the member and never handles the secret. Requires connection. A person owns a member, never a worker (ADR-135 D3), so each of these is REFUSED at load (boot, where the daemon does not start, and tera config apply) and at tera config plan, naming the member, the owner and which case it is: an owner that is not an email (a worker:<name> or any other principal), an email no user record claims, an email more than one record claims (never resolved by picking one, ADR-135 D11), and an email whose record is not a person. tera validate has no user directory, so it shape-checks the email and reports the member unresolvable, never resolved. One fact, one home: an owned member holds no copy of its credential, so grant {} and credential_provider {} are refused beside owner, and so is any provides entry that is a credential reference (env://, keychain://, vault://, secret://) or is named after its connection. No provides field maps to the connection; a provides entry left on an owned member is a non-secret literal. Load and plan judge EVERY member, not only one the change writes, so once an owner stops resolving the next boot, tera config apply and tera config plan all refuse until the owner or the directory is repaired, and plan says when the member is not that apply's edit. A daemon already running keeps serving: it resolves the owner afresh for every draw, and an owner changed, removed, or whose email stops resolving makes the member UNAVAILABLE at the next draw, with the reason on tera seats list, and it is never re-homed to another principal or treated as a team member. A record appearing later (a first login) resolves with no restart. Unset: a team member, which draws and reads its credential exactly as before. |
| `connection` | string | no | — | — | — | The declared connection this member's credential is for (ADR-148 D2, D7), by its credential key: a system-vault connection's bare stem, the name of its .tera/connections/<name>.hcl recipe, or a plugin installation's connection as plugin.<installation>/connections/<stem> — the key tera connections set takes, written the way a worker's connection block writes it. Either must have a token block, because a token is what tera connections set <connection> stores. REQUIRED beside owner: the owner's credential is their row for this connection. OPTIONAL on a team member, where it says what the member's own credential is for, so a work-order type's connection "<name>" { filer {} \| worker {} } choice for that connection governs the member (ADR-148 D3). A team member's credential is still its own — a reference, a grant {} or a value established with tera seats credential — supplied by the provides entry named after the connection (provides { <connection> = "..." }) — for a plugin connection, after its stem, since an attribute name cannot hold a / (connection = "plugin.anthropic/connections/claude-subscription" with provides { claude-subscription = "..." }) — which fills no capability field: the dispatch's proxy presents it as the connection's holder (ADR-152 D4). Its grant or established value is stored as (pool_member:<name>, <connection>); a reference is resolved where it lives. A team member that supplies a credential (a grant {}, a credential_provider {} or a credential reference in provides) MUST name the connection it is for when it sits in a pool for a tool whose toolchains declare connection blocks: one naming none is REFUSED at load and at tera config plan, naming the connections the toolchains apply and docs/ops/upgrade-to-connections.md, section Members name their connection (ADR-152 D4). A member in such a pool naming a connection none of the tool's toolchains applies is REFUSED the same way (ADR-152 D3). A team member supplying a credential for a tool whose toolchains declare no block may still name none. Every existing member row is read with no re-establishment. A member naming a connection no vault declares — a stem the system vault does not declare, or a plugin key whose installation is not installed or does not carry the stem — or one with no token block, is REFUSED at load and at tera config plan, naming the member and the connection. A member naming a connection whose recipe declares no proxy block can reach a session only through the seat overlay, which is raw delivery (ADR-148 D4): that connection must declare raw_delivery = true, or the member is REFUSED at load and at tera config plan, naming the member and the connection. |
| `credential_field` | string | no | — | — | — | REFUSED at load (boot and the reload guard), by tera validate and at tera config plan and apply, on every member, owned or team (ADR-152 D4). It named the capability credential_spec field the seat overlay filled with an owned member's credential, which put that credential in the sandbox. A member's credential now reaches only the dispatch's proxy, as the holder of the connection the member names, so there is no field to name. Remove it: an owned member keeps owner and connection, and a team member names connection = "<name>" and supplies provides { <name> = "..." }. The refusal names docs/ops/upgrade-to-connections.md, section Members name their connection, and credential_field is removed. The attribute stays decodable only so that refusal, rather than an unknown-argument error, is what an operator meets. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Free-form operator prose (whose subscription this is, which billing account pays for it, which device this names). |

## `provides` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## `grant` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `refresh_before` | string | no | — | — | — | How long before expiry to renew the grant (duration, e.g. 30m). Unset selects 30m. Sized so a dispatch never STARTS on a nearly-expired token; it cannot keep a long session alive, because an injected bearer cannot renew itself. |
| `token_url` | string | no | — | — | — | OAuth token endpoint override. Unset selects the endpoint the shipped Claude Code CLI uses. Set this only to work around a change on the provider's side. |
| `client_id` | string | no | — | — | — | OAuth client id override. Unset selects the shipped Claude Code CLI's, which is a PUBLIC client identifier (compiled into a binary every user has) and therefore not a credential reference. |

## `credential_provider` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | no | `paste` | — | — | Which provider establishes the credential: paste (default) prompts a person and accepts what they submit over the management API; command runs the declared program on the daemon host and reads the credential from its stdout. There is deliberately no device-code provider — no harness this deployment runs offers a device flow, and the durable human-step machinery one would need is what paste already exercises. |
| `field` | string | no | — | — | — | Which provides entry this provider establishes. Optional when the member supplies exactly one value; REQUIRED when it supplies more than one, and must name a declared entry. |
| `instructions` | string | no | — | — | — | What the operator is shown when the verb needs a person: the actual sentence they act on, rendered verbatim (e.g. "Run claude setup-token on your own machine and paste the token it prints"). Required for kind = paste, because a prompt with nothing to do is not a prompt. |
| `command` | string[] | no | — | — | — | argv of the program run for type = command. The credential is its stdout, whitespace-trimmed; a non-zero exit refuses and carries the program's stderr. Refused for type = paste, which runs nothing. |
| `timeout` | string | no | — | — | — | How long the provider gets (duration). For type = command it bounds the program; for type = paste it is how long the request waits for a person before it expires, which must be generous — an approval can take an hour. Unset selects 5m for command and 2h for paste. |
| `verify` | block | no | — | — | — | How the daemon proves the obtained credential actually works before it stores it and lifts the member's hold. REQUIRED: a provider that cannot demonstrate its result is not a provider, and a pasted token that does not work must not release a hold. |

## `credential_provider.verify` block

Nested under `credential_provider`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `command` | string[] | no | — | — | — | argv of the program run to prove the credential works, resolved on the daemon's own PATH. Exit 0 verifies; any other exit refuses and carries the program's stderr back to the operator. Use something that actually reaches the provider — a local status verb reports loggedIn for a string that is not a token and would pass on every input. Exactly one of command and bundled_tool is required. |
| `bundled_tool` | string | no | — | — | — | Name of a binary shipped beside tera by the package that installed it (e.g. "codex-handler"), resolved under this install's libexec at the moment the check runs. Use it instead of command when the check IS the packaged adapter: one spelling is then correct in a release archive, a Homebrew cellar, a container image and a development build alike. A bare filename only — never a path, and never a PATH search. Arguments go in args. |
| `args` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Arguments passed after the resolved bundled_tool path (e.g. ["verify-credential"]). Refused beside command, whose argv already carries its arguments. |
| `env` | string | no | — | — | — | Environment variable the candidate credential is injected into for the check. Unset selects the provides field name upper-cased (openai_api_key -> OPENAI_API_KEY). REQUIRED, and refused at load when unset, for a member whose provides entry is named after its connection (ADR-152 D4, provides { claude-subscription = "..." }): a connection's name is not a variable any program reads, so set the one the check's program reads — for a CLI, the variable its toolchain's connection "<name>" block sets (CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for claude-subscription and the claude CLI). Also required when the upper-cased field is not a usable variable name. |
| `timeout` | string | no | — | — | — | How long the check gets (duration). Unset selects 2m: long enough for a one-word completion and its retry ladder, short enough that the operator waiting on the verb is not left guessing. |
| `toolchain` | string | no | — | — | — | An ADR-109 toolchain whose env {} contributions are composed into the check's environment, so the check runs the pinned version (e.g. toolchain = "codex" supplies the absolute CODEX_EXECUTABLE). Unset composes nothing. The store must already be provisioned on this host — the check refuses rather than provisioning one, and never falls back to a PATH search. |
